title: 22. Interview: Docker
summary: Interview Q&A for Docker — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Docker interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a container, and how does it differ from a virtual machine?
**Answer:** A container is an isolated process (or group of processes) running on a host OS, with its own filesystem view, network namespace, process tree, and resource limits (cgroups), but sharing the host's kernel. A virtual machine (VM) is a full virtual computer — a hypervisor (VMware, KVM, Hyper-V) emulates hardware, and each VM runs a complete guest OS (its own kernel) on top. The differences are fundamental. **(1) Isolation mechanism.** VMs use hardware virtualization (a hypervisor presents virtual hardware to each VM); containers use OS-level virtualization (Linux namespaces restrict what a process can see; cgroups limit what it can use). VMs have stronger isolation (a VM escape requires a hypervisor bug; a container escape requires a kernel bug, and the kernel is shared). **(2) Startup time.** VMs boot a full OS (tens of seconds to minutes); containers start a process (milliseconds to seconds). **(3) Size.** VMs are gigabytes (full OS image); containers are megabytes (just the application and its libraries, sharing the host kernel). **(4) Density.** A single host runs maybe 10–50 VMs (each consumes dedicated RAM for its OS); a single host runs hundreds of containers (each is just a process). **(5) Portability.** A VM image runs on any hypervisor (portable across clouds); a Linux container runs on any Linux host with a compatible kernel (kernel version matters — a container built for kernel 5.x may not run on kernel 3.x). **(6) Use case.** VMs are best for strong isolation (multi-tenant, untrusted workloads, legacy apps needing a full OS); containers are best for high-density, fast-scaling microservices. In practice, the two are complementary — most containers run inside VMs (the VM provides isolation between tenants; the container provides density within a tenant), which is how all major clouds run Kubernetes.
**Visual:**
```
VIRTUAL MACHINE:                    CONTAINER:
  +---------+ +---------+            +---------+ +---------+ +---------+
  | App A   | | App B   |            | App A   | | App B   | | App C   |
  | Bins    | | Bins    |            | Bins    | | Bins    | | Bins    |
  | Libs    | | Libs    |            +----+----+ +----+----+ +----+----+
  +----+----+ +----+----+                 |           |           |
       |           |                       v           v           v
  +----+----+ +----+----+            +-----------------------------------+
  | Guest OS| | Guest OS|            | Docker Engine (container runtime) |
  | (kernel)| | (kernel)|            +-----------------+-----------------+
  +----+----+ +----+----+                              |
       |           |                                   v
  +----+-----------+----+            +-----------------------------------+
  |    Hypervisor     |            |           Host OS kernel           |
  +--------------------+            +-----------------+-----------------+
       |                                                 |
  +-----+-----+                                   +-----+-----+
  |  Host HW  |                                   |  Host HW  |
  +-----------+                                   +-----------+

  VM: full guest OS per VM, gigabytes, slow boot, strong isolation
  Container: shares host kernel, megabytes, ms boot, weaker (kernel-shared) isolation
  In practice: containers often run inside VMs (isolation + density)
```

### Q2. What is a Docker image, and how does layering work?
**Answer:** A Docker image is an immutable, versioned, layered filesystem artifact that contains everything needed to run an application: the application code, its runtime (Python, Java, Node), its libraries, its configuration, and a default command. The image is built up as a stack of **layers**, where each layer is a set of file diffs (additions, modifications, deletions) created by one instruction in the Dockerfile. The `FROM ubuntu:22.04` instruction pulls the Ubuntu base image (itself a stack of layers); `RUN apt-get install python3` creates a new layer with the installed packages; `COPY app.py /app/` creates a layer with the copied file; `CMD ["python3", "/app/app.py"]` adds metadata (no filesystem change). The image is the union of these layers, identified by a digest (a SHA256 hash of the layer contents and the parent chain). **Layering benefits.** (1) **Caching during build**: Docker caches each layer; if a Dockerfile instruction's inputs have not changed, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of re-running the instruction. This makes incremental builds fast (changing `app.py` rebuilds only layer 3, not layers 1 and 2). (2) **Sharing across images**: multiple images that share the same base layers (e.g., all Ubuntu-based images share the Ubuntu layers) store those layers only once on disk and in the registry. (3) **Fast container creation**: starting a container does not copy the image — it adds a thin read-write layer on top, and the container reads from the underlying layers (copy-on-write: the first write to a file copies it up to the read-write layer). **At runtime**, the container's filesystem is a union mount (OverlayFS) of the read-only image layers plus the read-write container layer. The image is immutable (you never modify it; you build a new version), but the container's read-write layer is mutable and ephemeral (destroyed when the container is removed).
**Visual:**
```
Dockerfile:                  Image (stack of layers, read-only):
  FROM ubuntu:22.04  ---->     layer 1: ubuntu base (80MB)         [shared]
  RUN apt-get install  ---->   layer 2: python3 + libs (40MB)      [cached]
  COPY app.py /app/   ---->    layer 3: app.py (5MB)
  CMD ["python3", ...] ---->   metadata: cmd (no fs change)

  image digest = sha256(layer1 + layer2 + layer3 + metadata)
  image is IMMUTABLE (build a new version, don't modify)

build caching:
  change app.py -> only layer 3 rebuilds (layers 1, 2 reused from cache)
  -> fast incremental builds

sharing across images:
  myapp:v1 (ubuntu + python + app)
  otherapp:v1 (ubuntu + python + other-app)
  -> ubuntu layer + python layer stored ONCE on disk and in registry

container (runtime):
  +---------------------+
  | read-write layer    |   (thin, ephemeral, destroyed on remove)
  | (copy-on-write)     |
  +---------------------+
  | image layers (RO)   |   (shared with other containers of same image)
  +---------------------+
  union mount (OverlayFS): reads check top first, writes copy up

  image is immutable; container's rw layer is mutable + ephemeral
```

### Q3. What is the Dockerfile, and how do you write an efficient one?
**Answer:** A Dockerfile is a text file with a sequence of instructions that Docker uses to build an image. Each instruction creates a layer (except metadata instructions like `CMD`, `ENV`, `LABEL`). The key instructions: `FROM` (base image), `RUN` (execute a command in a new layer), `COPY`/`ADD` (copy files from the build context into the image), `WORKDIR` (set working directory), `ENV` (set environment variable), `EXPOSE` (document a port), `CMD` (default command when container starts), `ENTRYPOINT` (the executable, with `CMD` as args). **Efficient Dockerfile principles.** (1) **Order instructions from least to most frequently changing.** Docker caches layers, and a cache miss invalidates all subsequent layers. Put stable steps (apt-get install) before volatile steps (COPY app code). If you `COPY app.py` before `RUN apt-get install`, every code change invalidates the apt layer and re-installs packages. (2) **Combine RUN instructions.** Each `RUN` creates a layer; combining `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` into one layer saves space and avoids leaking cached apt lists into the image. (3) **Use multi-stage builds.** Build the application in a full image (with compilers, build tools), then copy only the resulting binary into a minimal runtime image (scratch, distroless, alpine). This produces tiny images (10MB instead of 500MB) with no build tools exposed. (4) **Use a minimal base image.** `ubuntu:22.04` is 80MB; `python:3.11-slim` is 50MB; `python:3.11-alpine` is 40MB; `gcr.io/distroless/python3` is 20MB. Smaller images pull faster, attack surface is smaller. (5) **Don't run as root.** Add a non-root user (`USER appuser`) and run the container as that user — limits the blast radius of a container escape. (6) **Pin versions.** `FROM python:3.11.7-slim` (specific version) rather than `python:3` (floats, breaks reproducibility). (7) **Use .dockerignore.** Exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, `__pycache__`, large data files from the build context so they are not sent to the daemon.
**Visual:**
```
EFFICIENT Dockerfile (multi-stage, ordered for caching):

  # build stage (full image, has compilers)
  FROM golang:1.21 AS builder
  WORKDIR /src
  COPY go.mod go.sum ./         # deps first (rarely change)
  RUN go mod download           # cached unless go.mod changes
  COPY . .                      # app code (changes often)
  RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /app .

  # runtime stage (minimal, no compilers)
  FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
  COPY --from=builder /app /app
  USER nonroot
  ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

  result: 10MB image, no build tools, runs as non-root
  cache hits: change app code -> only COPY . . and RUN go build re-run

INEFFICIENT Dockerfile (anti-patterns):
  FROM ubuntu:22.04
  COPY app.py /app/             # WRONG: app code before apt -> cache miss
  RUN apt-get install python3   # re-runs on every code change
  RUN apt-get install -y curl   # WRONG: separate RUN -> 2 layers
  CMD python3 /app/app.py       # WRONG: runs as root

principles:
  (1) order: least-changing first (apt before COPY code)
  (2) combine RUN: apt update + install + cleanup in one layer
  (3) multi-stage: build in full, copy binary to minimal runtime
  (4) minimal base: distroless < alpine < slim < full
  (5) non-root USER
  (6) pin versions (python:3.11.7-slim, not python:3)
  (7) .dockerignore: exclude node_modules, .git, __pycache__, large files
```

### Q4. How do volumes work, and why are they needed?
**Answer:** Volumes are Docker's mechanism for persistent data — they store data outside the container's ephemeral read-write layer, so the data survives when the container is removed. The problem they solve: a container's filesystem (the read-write layer on top of the image layers) is destroyed when the container is removed. If a database writes to `/var/lib/postgresql/data` inside the container, that data is gone when the container is removed. Volumes fix this by mounting a storage location (managed by Docker, on the host, or networked) into the container at a path — writes to that path go to the volume, not the read-write layer, and persist beyond the container's life. **Three storage options in Docker.** (1) **Volumes** (`-v myvol:/data`): Docker-managed storage on the host (at `/var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol/_data`). Docker creates, manages, and cleans up the volume; the volume is independent of any container. Best for persistent application data (databases, logs). (2) **Bind mounts** (`-v /host/path:/container/path`): a specific host directory mounted into the container. The host path must exist; the container can read/write the host files directly. Useful for development (mount source code so changes are reflected immediately) but less portable (depends on host path). (3) **tmpfs mounts** (`--tmpfs /cache`): a RAM-backed filesystem, ephemeral (gone on container stop), for sensitive data (secrets) or fast ephemeral cache. **Volume lifecycle.** Volumes are created explicitly (`docker volume create myvol`) or implicitly (`docker run -v myvol:/data` creates the volume if it does not exist). They persist until explicitly removed (`docker volume rm myvol`). They can be shared across containers (mount the same volume in multiple containers). For production, networked volumes (NFS, AWS EFS, GlusterFS) allow data to be shared across hosts. In Kubernetes, this is abstracted as PersistentVolumeClaims, which bind to PersistentVolumes (cloud volumes like EBS, PD, or networked storage).
**Visual:**
```
PROBLEM (no volume):
  container writes to /var/lib/postgresql/data
  -> goes to read-write layer (ephemeral)
  -> container removed -> data GONE

SOLUTION (volume):
  docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
  -> /var/lib/postgresql/data in container maps to volume on host
  -> /var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data
  -> writes go to volume, NOT rw layer
  -> container removed -> volume persists -> new container can mount same volume

three storage options:
  (1) volume: -v myvol:/data
      Docker-managed, host path /var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol/_data
      + portable, Docker manages lifecycle
      + best for persistent app data (DBs, logs)
  (2) bind mount: -v /host/path:/container/path
      specific host directory mounted
      + dev use (mount source code, hot reload)
      - depends on host path, less portable
  (3) tmpfs: --tmpfs /cache
      RAM-backed, ephemeral (gone on container stop)
      + secrets, fast ephemeral cache
      - not persistent

volume lifecycle:
  docker volume create myvol (explicit) OR docker run -v myvol:/data (implicit)
  persists until docker volume rm myvol
  can be shared across containers (mount same volume in multiple)
  networked volumes (NFS, EFS, GlusterFS) for cross-host sharing
  in K8s: PersistentVolumeClaim -> PersistentVolume (EBS, PD, networked)
```

### Q5. What is the OCI standard, and why does it matter?
**Answer:** The OCI (Open Container Initiative) is a Linux Foundation project, founded in 2015 by Docker, CoreOS, Google, IBM, Microsoft, and others, to standardize the container format and runtime so that containers are not locked to Docker. It has three specifications. **(1) OCI Image Spec**: defines the image format — the manifest (a JSON document listing the image's layers and config), the config (a JSON document with the image's metadata: env vars, entrypoint, layers), and the layers (tar.gz archives of filesystem diffs). Any tool that produces OCI-compliant images (Docker, Buildah, Kaniko, podman, ko for Go) produces images that any OCI-compliant runtime can run. **(2) OCI Runtime Spec**: defines the runtime environment — what the container's config.json looks like (mounts, namespaces, cgroups, process), and what the runtime does to create and start a container. The reference implementation is **runc** (a CLI that takes a runtime bundle and starts a container), used by Docker, containerd, CRI-O. **(3) OCI Distribution Spec**: defines the registry API (how `docker pull` and `docker push` work), so any registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, GitHub Container Registry, Quay, Harbor) that implements the spec can serve images to any tool. **Why it matters.** Before OCI, Docker the company controlled the container format and runtime — lock-in. After OCI, the format and runtime are standardized and owned by the community. Docker the company can disappear (its enterprise business was sold to Mirantis in 2019), but Docker the technology survives because the format is open. You can build images with `buildah` (no Docker daemon), push them to any OCI registry, and run them with `runc` or `crun` or `kata-runtime` — none of which involve Docker, Inc. Kubernetes switched from Docker's runtime (dockershim) to containerd (an OCI runtime) in version 1.24 (2022) — the OCI standard made this seamless. The deeper principle is that open standards prevent vendor lock-in and ensure longevity — the OCI is why containers are a safe long-term bet.
**Visual:**
```
OCI (Open Container Initiative), founded 2015:
  standardizes container format + runtime so containers are not locked to Docker

three specs:
  (1) OCI Image Spec:
      image format: manifest (JSON, lists layers + config)
                    config (JSON, metadata: env, entrypoint, layers)
                    layers (tar.gz archives of fs diffs)
      tools that produce OCI images: Docker, Buildah, Kaniko, podman, ko
      -> any OCI runtime can run them

  (2) OCI Runtime Spec:
      runtime environment: config.json (mounts, namespaces, cgroups, process)
      reference impl: runc (CLI, takes runtime bundle, starts container)
      used by: Docker, containerd, CRI-O

  (3) OCI Distribution Spec:
      registry API (how docker pull/push work)
      registries: Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, GHCR, Quay, Harbor
      -> any tool can pull from any registry

why it matters:
  before OCI: Docker Inc. controlled format + runtime (lock-in)
  after OCI: format + runtime are community-owned standards
  Docker Inc. can disappear (enterprise sold to Mirantis 2019)
    -> Docker technology survives (format is open)
  build with buildah (no daemon), push to any registry, run with runc/crun
    -> no Docker Inc. involvement
  K8s switched from dockershim to containerd in v1.24 (2022) - seamless

  principle: open standards prevent vendor lock-in, ensure longevity
             OCI is why containers are a safe long-term bet
```

### Q6. How does Docker networking work — how do containers communicate with each other and with the outside world?
**Answer:** Docker networking is built on Linux network namespaces and virtual bridges. By default, Docker creates three networks when installed: **bridge** (the default — a virtual bridge `docker0` on the host, with containers getting IPs in the 172.17.0.0/16 range), **host** (the container uses the host's network namespace directly, no isolation — fast but no port isolation), and **none** (no networking). **How containers reach the outside world.** Each container gets its own network namespace with a virtual ethernet pair (one end in the container as `eth0`, the other on the host's `docker0` bridge). The container's traffic goes to `docker0`, which uses NAT (iptables MASQUERADE) to translate the container's private IP to the host's IP, so the container can reach the internet. **How the outside world reaches containers.** Port mapping: `docker run -p 8080:80` tells Docker to forward host port 8080 to container port 80 (via iptables DNAT). Traffic to `host-ip:8080` is forwarded to the container's port 80. **How containers communicate with each other.** On the default bridge network, containers can reach each other by IP (but not by name — the default bridge does not have DNS). For name-based discovery, create a user-defined bridge network (`docker network create mynet`) — Docker's embedded DNS resolves container names to IPs, so `docker run --network mynet --name app` can be reached as `app` from other containers on `mynet`. **For multi-host networking** (containers on different hosts), Docker Swarm's overlay network or third-party plugins (Flannel, Calico, Cilium) create a virtual network spanning hosts, using VXLAN or similar encapsulation. In Kubernetes, the Container Network Interface (CNI) handles this — each Pod gets a unique IP, and pods can communicate across nodes via the overlay network. **Trade-offs.** Bridge networking (default) is isolated and portable; host networking is faster (no NAT) but loses isolation; overlay networking (multi-host) adds overhead (VXLAN encapsulation, ~5% performance hit). For most applications, the default bridge with user-defined networks for service discovery is the right choice; in Kubernetes, the CNI plugin handles all of this transparently.
**Visual:**
```
Docker networking (default bridge):

  +-----------------------------------------------------------+
  | HOST                                                       |
  |                                                           |
  |   +-------------+      +-------------+                    |
  |   | container A |      | container B |                    |
  |   | eth0:       |      | eth0:       |                    |
  |   | 172.17.0.2  |      | 172.17.0.3  |                    |
  |   +------+------+      +------+------+                    |
  |          |                    |                            |
  |   +------v--------------------v------+                    |
  |   |   docker0 bridge (172.17.0.1)   |                    |
  |   +---------------+-----------------+                    |
  |                   |                                       |
  |           +-------v-------+         +-----------+         |
  |           | NAT (iptables)|<------->| host eth0 |         |
  |           | MASQUERADE    |         | (public)  |         |
  |           +-------+-------+         +-----+-----+         |
  |                   |                       |               |
  |           -p 8080:80 (DNAT, port mapping) |               |
  |           host:8080 -> containerA:80      |               |
  +-------------------------------------------|---------------+
                                              v
                                          INTERNET

  container -> outside:  container eth0 -> docker0 -> NAT -> host eth0 -> internet
  outside -> container:  host:8080 -> DNAT -> containerA:80 (port mapping)
  container <-> container (default bridge): by IP only (no DNS)
  container <-> container (user-defined bridge): by name (DNS resolves)
    docker network create mynet; docker run --network mynet --name app
    other containers on mynet can reach as "app"

  multi-host (overlay, Swarm or CNI plugin):
    containers on different hosts, virtual network via VXLAN
    K8s uses CNI (Flannel, Calico, Cilium) -> each pod unique IP, cross-node

  trade-offs:
    bridge (default): isolated, portable, name resolution in user-defined
    host network: faster (no NAT), no isolation
    overlay (multi-host): VXLAN overhead (~5% perf hit)
```

### Q7. What are the security risks of running containers, and how do you mitigate them?
**Answer:** Containers share the host kernel, which is the source of their main security risk: a kernel vulnerability or a misconfigured container can allow an attacker to escape the container and access the host or other containers. The mitigations form a defense-in-depth strategy. **(1) Run as non-root.** By default, containers run as root (UID 0 inside the container, which maps to root on the host unless user namespaces are used). Add a non-root user in the Dockerfile (`RUN useradd -m appuser && USER appuser`) and run as that user — limits the blast radius of an escape. **(2) Drop capabilities.** Linux capabilities partition root's privileges into ~40 distinct units. By default, Docker drops many but grants some (CHOWN, NET_BIND_SERVICE). Use `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` to drop everything and add only what is needed. **(3) Use seccomp profiles.** Seccomp filters which syscalls a container can make. Docker's default profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls (like `kexec_load`, `reboot`); custom profiles can block more. **(4) Use AppArmor or SELinux.** These MAC (mandatory access control) systems add another layer of access control — a container's processes can only access resources the policy allows, even if they escape the container. **(5) Use user namespaces.** User namespace mapping remaps UID 0 inside the container to a non-root UID on the host — so even if an attacker escapes the container, they are a non-root user on the host. **(6) Read-only filesystem.** `--read-only` makes the container's root filesystem read-only (writes must go to explicit volumes), limiting where an attacker can drop payloads. **(7) Resource limits.** Set CPU and memory limits (`--cpus`, `--memory`) so a runaway container cannot starve the host (DoS). **(8) Scan images for vulnerabilities.** Tools like Trivy, Snyk, Clair scan images for known CVEs in their packages; integrate into CI to block vulnerable images. **(9) Pin image digests, not tags.** `myapp@sha256:abc...` instead of `myapp:v1` — tags are mutable (an attacker who pushes a malicious `v1` would be pulled), digests are immutable. **(10) For multi-tenant or untrusted workloads, use stronger isolation** — gVisor (a user-space kernel), Kata Containers (a container in a lightweight VM), or just use VMs. The deeper principle is defense-in-depth — no single measure is sufficient, but layered together they reduce the attack surface significantly.
**Visual:**
```
container security risks:
  - shares host kernel (kernel vuln = escape)
  - default: runs as root (UID 0)
  - default: some capabilities granted
  - image vulnerabilities (CVEs in packages)
  - mutable tags (attacker can replace v1)

defense-in-depth mitigations:
  (1) non-root USER in Dockerfile (USER appuser)
  (2) drop capabilities: --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE
  (3) seccomp profile (default blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls)
  (4) AppArmor / SELinux (MAC, another access control layer)
  (5) user namespaces (UID 0 in container -> non-root on host)
  (6) read-only root fs: --read-only (writes to explicit volumes only)
  (7) resource limits: --cpus 1.0 --memory 512m (prevent DoS)
  (8) image scanning (Trivy, Snyk, Clair) in CI, block vulnerable images
  (9) pin by digest: myapp@sha256:abc... (immutable, not mutable tag)
  (10) for untrusted workloads: gVisor, Kata Containers, or VMs

  example hardened run:
    docker run --read-only \
      --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
      --security-opt no-new-privileges \
      --security-opt seccomp=profile.json \
      --user 1000:1000 \
      --cpus 1.0 --memory 512m \
      --tmpfs /tmp \
      -v data:/data \
      myapp@sha256:abc123...

  principle: defense-in-depth, no single measure sufficient
             layered together -> significantly reduced attack surface
             for multi-tenant / untrusted -> VMs or Kata/gVisor
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team builds a Python service. The Docker image is 1.2 GB and takes 5 minutes to build. How do you make it smaller and faster?
**Answer:** A 1.2 GB Python image is usually the result of using a full base image (`python:3.11` is ~900 MB) plus build tools left in the image plus poor layer caching. Four interventions. **(1) Use a slim or alpine base.** Replace `FROM python:3.11` (900 MB) with `FROM python:3.11-slim` (50 MB, no build tools) or `FROM python:3.11-alpine` (40 MB, musl libc — may need package changes). For maximum minimalism, use `gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12` (20 MB, no shell, no package manager — very secure). **(2) Multi-stage build.** Build dependencies in a full image (with gcc, build-essential for compiling C extensions), then copy only the installed packages to a slim runtime image. The build tools stay in the build stage, not the runtime image. **(3) Order Dockerfile for caching.** Copy `requirements.txt` and `pip install` BEFORE copying the application code. Code changes frequently; requirements change rarely. If you `COPY . .` before `pip install`, every code change invalidates the pip layer and re-installs all packages (slow). **(4) Use a build cache.** Docker BuildKit (default in modern Docker) caches pip downloads across builds — `pip install --no-cache-dir` reduces image size but slows rebuilds; use BuildKit's cache mounts (`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt`) for fast rebuilds without bloating the image. **(5) Combine RUN instructions and clean up.** `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in one layer avoids leaking apt lists. **(6) Use .dockerignore.** Exclude `node_modules`, `.git`, `__pycache__`, `*.pyc`, large data files, the `.venv` directory from the build context — they are sent to the daemon on every build, slowing it down. **Result.** A typical Python service image drops from 1.2 GB to ~100 MB (slim) or ~50 MB (alpine with multi-stage), and build time drops from 5 minutes to under 1 minute (with caching).
**Visual:**
```
BEFORE (1.2GB image, 5 min build):
  FROM python:3.11                # 900MB base (full)
  COPY . /app                     # all code (including .git, .venv)
  RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # gcc + build tools left in image
  CMD python /app/app.py          # runs as root

AFTER (100MB image, <1 min build):
  # build stage (full, has compilers)
  FROM python:3.11 AS builder
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY requirements.txt .         # deps first (rarely change, cached)
  RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
      pip install --user -r requirements.txt
  COPY . .                        # app code (changes often, only this rebuilds)

  # runtime stage (slim, no compilers)
  FROM python:3.11-slim           # 50MB base
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
  COPY --from=builder /app /app
  ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
  USER 1000:1000                  # non-root
  CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"]

  # .dockerignore:
  .git
  __pycache__
  *.pyc
  .venv
  node_modules
  *.sqlite

  result: ~100MB image (slim) or ~50MB (alpine), <1 min build with caching
```

### Q2. You have a Node.js service that needs to be deployed. The team is debating whether to use Docker or just deploy via PM2 (a Node process manager) on a VM. How do you decide?
**Answer:** The decision depends on scale, team expertise, and operational maturity. **Use PM2 on a VM when.** (1) Single service, simple deployment — PM2 starts the Node process, restarts on crash, manages logs, and you have one VM per service. (2) Small team without container expertise — the operational overhead of Docker (Dockerfiles, registries, image scanning, orchestration) may not be worth it for a single service. (3) Tight coupling to the OS — if the service needs specific OS packages or kernel tuning that is easier to manage on a VM. (4) Low deployment frequency — if you deploy monthly, the speed advantage of Docker (seconds vs minutes) is irrelevant. **Use Docker when.** (1) Multiple services — Docker's portability (same image runs anywhere) and density (many containers per host) shine as the service count grows. (2) Microservices architecture — Docker is the deployment unit that Kubernetes orchestrates; if you are heading toward microservices, start with Docker. (3) Environment parity — Docker images run identically in dev, staging, prod; PM2 on VMs suffers environment drift (different Node versions, different OS packages across environments). (4) CI/CD pipeline — Docker images are versioned artifacts that flow through CI (build, test, scan) to CD (deploy); PM2 deploys are SSH-and-pull, harder to make reproducible. (5) Scaling — Docker (with Kubernetes or ECS) scales by adding containers in seconds; PM2 on VMs scales by adding VMs (minutes) via an ASG. **The pragmatic path.** For a team starting with one Node service and uncertain about future scale: start with PM2 on a VM (simple, fast to set up), but write the service to be containerizable (no OS-specific dependencies, configurable via env vars, health-checkable). When the second or third service arrives, or when environment drift causes incidents, migrate to Docker. The migration is mechanical (write a Dockerfile, push to a registry, deploy via compose or ECS) if the service is container-friendly from the start.
**Visual:**
```
DECISION: Docker vs PM2 on VM for a Node.js service

  USE PM2 ON VM WHEN:
    - single service, simple deployment (one VM per service)
    - small team without container expertise
    - tight OS coupling (specific packages, kernel tuning)
    - low deployment frequency (monthly -> speed irrelevant)

  USE DOCKER WHEN:
    - multiple services (portability + density shine at scale)
    - microservices architecture (Docker is K8s's deployment unit)
    - environment parity needed (image runs identically dev/staging/prod)
    - CI/CD pipeline (versioned artifacts, reproducible deploys)
    - scaling (containers in seconds vs VMs in minutes)

  PRAGMATIC PATH (for uncertain scale):
    start with PM2 on VM (simple, fast setup)
    but write service to be containerizable:
      - no OS-specific dependencies
      - configurable via env vars (not hardcoded paths)
      - health-checkable (/health endpoint)
      - graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handler)
    when 2nd/3rd service arrives or env drift causes incidents:
      migrate to Docker (mechanical: Dockerfile, registry, compose/ECS)

  trade-off summary:
    PM2: + simple, no container overhead, direct OS access
         - env drift, slower scaling, harder CI/CD, single-service focus
    Docker: + portable, fast scaling, CI/CD-friendly, microservices-ready
            - container expertise needed, orchestration overhead (K8s/ECS)
```

### Q3. A container in production is using 4 GB of memory but the host only has 2 GB free. The container is being OOM-killed. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** An OOM (Out of Memory) kill means the container's processes exceeded their memory limit (or the host's memory), and the kernel killed the process to protect the host. Three layers of investigation and fix. **(1) Set explicit memory limits.** If you did not set `--memory` (or resources.limits.memory in K8s), the container can use all available host memory — and the kernel's OOM killer may kill any process on the host (not just the container). Always set a memory limit: `docker run --memory=2g` (the container is OOM-killed if it exceeds 2 GB, protecting the host and other containers). In K8s, set both `resources.requests.memory` (for scheduling) and `resources.limits.memory` (the hard cap). **(2) Investigate the memory usage.** Why is the container using 4 GB? Common causes: (a) a memory leak in the application (a growing cache, unreleased references); profile the application with language-specific tools (heap dumps, `pmap`, `jmap`). (b) The application's memory settings are too high (JVM heap size `-Xmx4g`, Node `--max-old-space-size=4096`); reduce them to fit the limit. (c) The container is running multiple processes (e.g., a web server + a worker), each with its own memory needs; split into separate containers. (d) A large dataset loaded into memory (a 3 GB CSV parsed in one go); stream it instead. **(3) Right-size the limit.** The limit should be set to the application's actual memory needs plus headroom — measure under realistic load (the 95th percentile memory usage), then add 20–30% headroom. Too low: OOM kills under load spikes. Too high: wastes resources, host can run fewer containers. **(4) Handle OOM gracefully.** The application should handle SIGTERM (Docker sends SIGTERM on stop, SIGKILL after grace period) to shut down cleanly. For OOM specifically, the container will be killed — set a restart policy (`docker run --restart unless-stopped`, or K8s Deployment which restarts automatically) and ensure the application starts up cleanly (no corrupted state from the kill). **(5) Monitor and alert.** Track container memory usage (Prometheus cAdvisor metrics) and alert when usage exceeds 80% of the limit — catch the leak before the OOM kill.
**Visual:**
```
PROBLEM: container using 4GB, host has 2GB free -> OOM-killed

  INVESTIGATION + FIX:

  (1) set explicit memory limit:
      docker run --memory=2g (or K8s: resources.limits.memory: 2Gi)
      + container is OOM-killed (not host processes) if it exceeds
      + protects host and other containers
      - too low: OOM kills under load spikes
      - too high: wastes resources

  (2) investigate why 4GB:
      (a) memory leak: profile with heap dump, pmap, jmap
          -> fix the leak (release references, bound caches)
      (b) app memory settings too high:
          JVM -Xmx4g -> reduce to -Xmx2g
          Node --max-old-space-size=4096 -> reduce
      (c) multiple processes in one container:
          split into separate containers (one process per container)
      (d) large dataset in memory:
          stream it instead of loading all at once

  (3) right-size the limit:
      measure 95th percentile memory under realistic load
      add 20-30% headroom
      too low: OOM under spikes; too high: wastes resources

  (4) handle OOM gracefully:
      SIGTERM handler in app (clean shutdown)
      restart policy: --restart unless-stopped (or K8s Deployment auto-restart)
      ensure clean startup (no corrupted state from kill)

  (5) monitor and alert:
      track container memory (Prometheus cAdvisor)
      alert when usage > 80% of limit
      -> catch leak BEFORE OOM kill
```

### Q4. You need to deploy a stateful service (a Redis cache with persistence) on Docker. How do you handle the data?
**Answer:** Redis with persistence (AOF or RDB) writes to disk — if the writes go to the container's ephemeral read-write layer, the data is lost when the container is removed. The fix is a volume. **(1) Use a named volume for Redis's data directory.** `docker run -v redisdata:/data redis` mounts a Docker-managed volume at `/data` (Redis's default data directory); writes go to the volume, which persists beyond the container's life. When you remove the container and start a new one with the same volume, Redis loads the persisted data. **(2) Configure Redis persistence.** Set `--appendonly yes` (AOF, every write logged) or `--save 60 1000` (RDB, snapshot every 60s if 1000+ keys changed) via Redis config or command-line args. AOF is more durable (less data loss on crash); RDB is faster (less write overhead). For a cache, RDB is usually sufficient; for a session store or any data you cannot lose, AOF. **(3) Back up the volume.** Volumes persist on the host, but if the host dies, the volume dies with it. For production: (a) use a volume backed by networked storage (EFS, NFS) that is replicated across availability zones; or (b) schedule periodic backups (snapshot the volume, copy to S3); or (c) use Redis replication (a primary + replicas) so the data is on multiple hosts. **(4) For high availability, use Redis Sentinel or Redis Cluster.** Sentinel monitors the primary and promotes a replica on failure. Cluster shards data across multiple primaries (each with replicas). Both run as multiple containers with their own volumes, coordinated. **(5) In Kubernetes, use a StatefulSet with a PersistentVolumeClaim.** The PVC binds to a PersistentVolume (EBS, PD, or networked storage); the StatefulSet ensures the Pod is rescheduled with the same volume on restart. For Redis specifically, consider a managed service (Elasticache, Memorystore) — running stateful services in containers is operationally complex, and managed services handle backups, replication, failover, and patching for you.
**Visual:**
```
PROBLEM: Redis with persistence, data must survive container removal

  SOLUTION: volume + persistence config

  (1) named volume for Redis data dir:
      docker run -v redisdata:/data redis
      -> /data maps to /var/lib/docker/volumes/redisdata/_data (host)
      -> writes go to volume, NOT ephemeral rw layer
      -> container removed, new container mounts same volume -> data persists

  (2) configure Redis persistence:
      docker run -v redisdata:/data redis \
        redis-server --appendonly yes          # AOF (every write logged)
      OR
      docker run -v redisdata:/data redis \
        redis-server --save 60 1000            # RDB (snapshot every 60s)
      AOF: more durable (less loss on crash), slower
      RDB: faster, less durable
      cache: RDB usually sufficient
      session store / can't-lose: AOF

  (3) back up the volume:
      volume on host -> if host dies, volume dies
      production options:
        (a) networked storage (EFS, NFS) replicated across AZs
        (b) periodic snapshots to S3
        (c) Redis replication (primary + replicas) -> data on multiple hosts

  (4) high availability:
      Redis Sentinel: monitors primary, promotes replica on failure
      Redis Cluster: shards across primaries (each with replicas)
      -> multiple containers with own volumes, coordinated

  (5) in Kubernetes:
      StatefulSet + PersistentVolumeClaim
      PVC binds to PersistentVolume (EBS, PD, networked)
      StatefulSet ensures Pod rescheduled with same volume on restart

  PREFER MANAGED (Elasticache, Memorystore) for production Redis:
      running stateful in containers is operationally complex
      managed handles backups, replication, failover, patching
```

### Q5. Your CI pipeline builds a Docker image, tags it `myapp:latest`, and pushes to the registry. Production pulls `myapp:latest`. What's wrong with this, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** Using `:latest` (or any mutable tag) for production is a well-known anti-pattern with several serious problems. **(1) No reproducibility.** `:latest` is mutable — it points to whatever was most recently pushed. If you deploy `:latest` today and again tomorrow, you may get different images (a new build was pushed in between). You cannot reproduce a deployment — "what version is running in prod?" has no reliable answer. **(2) No rollback.** If `:latest` is broken, rolling back means "push the old image as `:latest` again" — but the old image may have been overwritten. You cannot say "roll back to yesterday's `:latest`" because that tag now points to today's broken image. **(3) Caching ambiguity.** Docker pulls cache by tag — if `:latest` is already present on a host, `docker pull myapp:latest` may use the cached image (not the newly pushed one), depending on the pull policy. This leads to "I deployed but the new code is not running" debugging nightmares. **(4) No audit trail.** "We deployed `:latest` at 14:32" tells you nothing about which commit, which build, which dependencies were in that image. **The fix.** (1) **Tag images with immutable identifiers** — the Git commit SHA (`myapp:abc1234`), the build number (`myapp:build-42`), or a semantic version (`myapp:v1.4.2`). These tags are immutable (you never re-tag the same identifier). (2) **Pin by digest in production.** Even an immutable tag can be re-pushed (rare but possible); pin by digest for full immutability: `myapp@sha256:abc123...`. The digest is a content hash of the image; it cannot change without the image changing. Production manifests reference the digest. (3) **CI tags automatically.** CI tags the image with the commit SHA and the build number, pushes both tags. (4) **Deploy by referencing the specific tag/digest.** The deploy pipeline updates the production manifest (K8s Deployment, ECS task definition) to reference the new image tag/digest; this is the unit of deployment, and it is auditable (which commit, which build, when). (5) **Never use `:latest`** except for local development convenience. In production, ban it via policy (admission controller, CI lint).
**Visual:**
```
PROBLEM: tag :latest, mutable, no reproducibility

  CI: build -> tag myapp:latest -> push
  prod: pull myapp:latest

  issues:
    (1) no reproducibility: :latest points to most recent push
        deploy today vs tomorrow -> different images
        "what version is in prod?" -> no reliable answer
    (2) no rollback: :latest overwritten, can't roll back to "yesterday's :latest"
    (3) caching ambiguity: docker pull may use cached :latest
        -> "deployed but new code not running"
    (4) no audit trail: "deployed :latest at 14:32" -> which commit? which build?

  FIX:
  (1) tag with immutable identifiers:
      myapp:abc1234     (Git commit SHA)
      myapp:build-42    (build number)
      myapp:v1.4.2      (semantic version)
      -> never re-tag the same identifier
  (2) pin by digest in production:
      myapp@sha256:abc123...   (content hash, fully immutable)
      -> production manifests reference digest
  (3) CI tags automatically:
      commit SHA + build number, pushes both
  (4) deploy by specific tag/digest:
      deploy pipeline updates K8s Deployment / ECS task def
      -> auditable (which commit, which build, when)
  (5) never use :latest in production:
      ban via policy (admission controller, CI lint)
      :latest only for local dev convenience
```

### Q6. You have a Docker image that works on your Mac (M1, ARM64) but fails in production (Linux x86_64) with "exec format error." How do you fix this?
**Answer:** "exec format error" means the binary in the image is for the wrong CPU architecture — the image was built for ARM64 (Apple M1) but production is x86_64 (Intel/AMD), and the kernel cannot execute an ARM64 binary on an x86_64 host. Three solutions. **(1) Build for the target architecture explicitly.** Use `docker build --platform linux/amd64` to build an x86_64 image on your M1 Mac (Docker uses QEMU emulation to run the x86_64 build). The resulting image runs on production. Trade-off: emulation is slow (5–10x slower than native builds). **(2) Multi-arch builds with buildx.** Use Docker BuildKit's `buildx` to build multi-architecture images — a single `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t myapp:v1 --push` builds both architectures and pushes them as a single manifest list. When production pulls `myapp:v1`, the registry serves the right architecture based on the host's platform. This is the best solution: one image tag, two architectures, the registry handles the selection. The build can use QEMU (slow) or native builders (fast — run an amd64 builder on an amd64 host and an arm64 builder on an arm64 host, buildx orchestrates both). **(3) Use a CI runner with the target architecture.** Run CI on an x86_64 runner (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) that builds the image natively — no emulation, fast, and the image is for the right architecture. This is the most common production setup: developers build on Macs (M1 or Intel), CI builds the production image on an x86_64 runner. **The deeper lesson.** Architecture mismatches are a portability issue that Docker's image format makes explicit — the image's manifest declares its architecture (`linux/amd64` or `linux/arm64`), and the runtime checks compatibility. Multi-arch images (manifest lists) solve this cleanly — build once, run anywhere, on any architecture. As ARM servers (AWS Graviton, Ampere) become common for cost reasons, multi-arch builds are increasingly the default rather than the exception.
**Visual:**
```
PROBLEM: image built on Mac M1 (ARM64), prod is x86_64
  -> "exec format error" (kernel can't run ARM64 binary on x86_64 host)

  Mac M1 builds: myapp:v1 (linux/arm64)
  prod pulls: myapp:v1 -> tries to run ARM64 binary -> exec format error

  SOLUTIONS:

  (1) build for target arch explicitly:
      docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t myapp:v1 .
      -> Docker uses QEMU emulation to run x86_64 build on M1
      -> resulting image runs on production (x86_64)
      trade-off: emulation is slow (5-10x slower than native)

  (2) multi-arch builds with buildx (BEST):
      docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
        -t myapp:v1 --push
      -> builds both architectures, pushes as single manifest list
      -> prod pulls myapp:v1 -> registry serves amd64 variant
      -> Mac pulls myapp:v1 -> registry serves arm64 variant
      build can use QEMU (slow) or native builders (fast):
        amd64 builder on amd64 host + arm64 builder on arm64 host
        buildx orchestrates both

  (3) CI runner with target arch:
      CI runs on x86_64 runner (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI)
      builds image natively (no emulation, fast, right arch)
      -> most common production setup:
         devs build on Macs (M1 or Intel)
         CI builds production image on x86_64 runner

  lesson: Docker image manifest declares architecture (linux/amd64 or arm64)
          runtime checks compatibility
          multi-arch images (manifest lists) solve this cleanly
          as ARM servers (Graviton, Ampere) become common for cost,
          multi-arch builds are increasingly the default
```

### Q7. Your team is moving to microservices and wants to containerize all of them. What's your containerization strategy and rollout plan?
**Answer:** Containerizing a fleet of microservices is a multi-phase migration, not a big-bang. The strategy has four phases. **(1) Establish container standards (week 1–2).** Define a base image standard (e.g., distroless or alpine for the runtime stage), a Dockerfile template (multi-stage, non-root user, health check, pinned versions), a .dockerignore template, a registry (ECR, GCR, Harbor), and an image tagging policy (commit SHA + build number, never `:latest`). Document these in a shared repo so all teams follow the same pattern. **(2) Containerize one pilot service (week 3–4).** Pick a low-risk, stateless service (e.g., a read-only API). Write its Dockerfile, set up CI to build and push the image, deploy it via Docker Compose or a single-node Docker setup (no orchestration yet). Work through the operational details: logging (stdout, picked up by a log driver), configuration (env vars, mounted ConfigMaps), health checks (liveness, readiness), graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handler). The pilot proves the pattern and surfaces issues before scaling. **(3) Add orchestration (week 5–8).** Stand up Kubernetes (or ECS, Nomad) — managed (EKS, GKE) is strongly preferred over self-hosted. Migrate the pilot service to K8s. Define the deployment manifests (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, Ingress). Set up CI/CD to deploy images to K8s (GitOps with ArgoCD is the cleanest pattern). Work through the operational details: monitoring (Prometheus), logging (Loki/ELK), tracing (Jaeger), alerting. **(4) Migrate the rest of the services (week 9+).** Each service follows the standard Dockerfile template and manifests. Migrate incrementally — one or two services per week, with a canary deployment (1% traffic first, watch metrics, ramp). For stateful services (databases), prefer managed services (RDS, Elasticache) over containerized stateful workloads — the operational complexity is rarely worth it. **(5) Decommission the old infrastructure.** Once all services are on K8s, shut down the VMs or the old deployment system. **The key principles.** Standardize early (one Dockerfile template, one manifest pattern, one CI/CD pipeline) — variation is the enemy of scale. Migrate incrementally (don't big-bang) — each migration is a learning opportunity. Prefer managed services for state — don't containerize databases. Invest in observability from day one — debugging containers without metrics/logs/traces is painful.
**Visual:**
```
CONTAINERIZATION STRATEGY + ROLLOUT (multi-phase migration):

  (1) ESTABLISH STANDARDS (week 1-2):
      base image: distroless or alpine (runtime stage)
      Dockerfile template: multi-stage, non-root, health check, pinned versions
      .dockerignore template
      registry: ECR, GCR, Harbor
      tagging policy: commit SHA + build number, NEVER :latest
      document in shared repo -> all teams follow same pattern

  (2) PILOT SERVICE (week 3-4):
      pick low-risk, stateless service (read-only API)
      write Dockerfile, CI builds + pushes image
      deploy via Docker Compose (no orchestration yet)
      work through ops details:
        logging (stdout, log driver picks up)
        config (env vars, mounted files)
        health checks (liveness, readiness)
        graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handler)
      -> pilot proves pattern, surfaces issues

  (3) ADD ORCHESTRATION (week 5-8):
      stand up K8s (managed: EKS/GKE preferred over self-hosted)
      migrate pilot to K8s
      manifests: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, Ingress
      CI/CD: GitOps with ArgoCD (cleanest pattern)
      observability: Prometheus (metrics), Loki/ELK (logs), Jaeger (traces)
      alerting on service SLOs

  (4) MIGRATE REST (week 9+):
      each service follows standard template + manifests
      incremental: 1-2 services per week
      canary deploy (1% traffic first, watch metrics, ramp)
      stateful services (DBs): PREFER MANAGED (RDS, Elasticache)
        -> don't containerize databases (ops complexity rarely worth it)

  (5) DECOMMISSION OLD INFRA:
      once all on K8s, shut down VMs / old deployment system

  KEY PRINCIPLES:
    - standardize early (one Dockerfile template, one manifest pattern, one CI/CD)
      variation is the enemy of scale
    - migrate incrementally (don't big-bang)
      each migration is a learning opportunity
    - prefer managed for state (don't containerize DBs)
    - invest in observability from day one
      debugging containers without metrics/logs/traces is painful
```
